explanations.answer: Into the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right there, friend. Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and walks straight into the house of the LORD (2 Kings 19:1). Bad news lands, and he heads for the LORD's house. Some of us head for the fridge, but I only deal in cookies.

The city wall is a fine place to check on trouble, but that's not where the text sends him. It says he "entered the house of the LORD." Same torn clothes and sackcloth, but he's heading somewhere a lot better than a wall.
Counting coins wouldn't have fixed this one, and the text never has him try. It says Hezekiah "entered the house of the LORD." I think a king in sackcloth knows a money problem from a LORD problem.

Isaiah son of Amoz is the one. Hezekiah sends Eliakim, Shebna and the leading priests, all in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah (2 Kings 19:2). That's a whole delegation showing up at one prophet's door.

Elisha son of Shaphat is a prophet in Scripture (2 Kings 3:11), but he's not the one named here. The text sends the officials and priests to "the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz." Wrong door, same sackcloth.

Jeremiah son of Hilkiah is a prophet too (Jeremiah 1:1, 5), but he isn't who Hezekiah's men go to see. The verse says they go "to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz." Easy to mix up when the names pile up.
Prayer is it. Hezekiah says, "Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives." (2 Kings 19:4) He asks the prophet to pray for the people who are still left.
A banner is something you wave, and nobody's waving anything here. Hezekiah asks Isaiah to "lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives." (2 Kings 19:4) What he needs lifted is a prayer.
A sword would be a very different request, friend. Hezekiah asks Isaiah to "lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives." (2 Kings 19:4) He's asking for prayer, not for weapons.

Land is right. The LORD says Sennacherib will hear a rumor and "return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword." (2 Kings 19:7) Hezekiah has barely finished worrying and the LORD already has the ending.
Close, but a camp is only where he's staying for now. The LORD says the king will "return to his own land." (2 Kings 19:7) That's a whole country, not a tent.
A fleet doesn't show up anywhere in these verses. The LORD says the king will hear a rumor and "return to his own land." (2 Kings 19:7) Nobody's boarding a boat in this story.
The text says the opposite. After Sennacherib hears about Tirhakah, king of Cush, he "again sent messengers to Hezekiah." (2 Kings 19:9) Having another army coming doesn't make him drop his threats.

That's right. Sennacherib hears Tirhakah, king of Cush, has set out to fight him, and he still sends messengers to Hezekiah again (2 Kings 19:9). He's got a new worry and he's still barking at Jerusalem. Some folks just can't leave a letter unsent.

That's his whole point. He tells Hezekiah, "Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria." (2 Kings 19:10) Then he lists the nations and their gods, as if they all lost, so Hezekiah's God will lose too.

It's the opposite of False. Sennacherib says not to let Hezekiah's God deceive him into thinking Jerusalem won't be delivered into Assyria's hand (2 Kings 19:10). Then he points at the gods of Gozan, Haran, Rezeph and Eden in Telassar (2 Kings 19:12). His message is that Jerusalem is next.

explanations.answer: Spreads it out before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. Hezekiah read the letter, went up to the house of the LORD, and "spread it out before the LORD." (2 Kings 19:14) He takes the whole threat and lays it right there in front of Him.
No fire in this scene, friend. The text says Hezekiah "spread it out before the LORD." (2 Kings 19:14) The letter stays in one piece, and he sets it where the LORD can see it.
He already tore his clothes earlier (2 Kings 19:1), but the letter gets different treatment. Hezekiah "spread it out before the LORD." (2 Kings 19:14) Nothing in the verse says he rips it.

True. Hezekiah prays, "O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth." (2 Kings 19:15) He's got the Maker of everything in front of him, and he says so first.

He says it, so it's True. In the opening of his prayer, Hezekiah tells the LORD, "You made the heavens and the earth." (2 Kings 19:15) That's right alongside "You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth."
True. Hezekiah prays, "Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste these nations and their lands." (2 Kings 19:17) He doesn't dodge the hard part. He names it out loud to the LORD.

Hezekiah doesn't deny it, so it's True. His prayer says, "Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste these nations and their lands." (2 Kings 19:17) He tells the LORD the facts plainly before he asks for anything.

explanations.answer: They were only wood and stone
explanations.explanation: Right on. Hezekiah says Assyria cast those gods into the fire "for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands." (2 Kings 19:18) If hands made it, a fire can finish it.

The text gives a different reason. Hezekiah says they were destroyed "for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands." (2 Kings 19:18) It's about what those gods were, not what people felt about them.

Surrender isn't mentioned in his prayer. Hezekiah says the gods went into the fire "for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands." (2 Kings 19:18) That's the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: So all kingdoms know the LORD alone is God
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. Hezekiah asks, "please save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God." (2 Kings 19:19) He wants more than his own city safe. He wants the whole earth to know who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: So Judah can finally rule over Assyria
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah never asks for that. His reason is "so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God." (2 Kings 19:19) Ruling over anyone isn't in the prayer.

explanations.answer: So the people keep trusting their king
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says. Hezekiah prays for salvation "so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God." (2 Kings 19:19) He's pointing everybody to the LORD, not to himself.

True. The LORD's word says, "The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you." (2 Kings 19:21) Sennacherib was loud for a long time, and now the shaking head is aimed at him.
The text says otherwise, so it's True. The LORD's word says, "The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you." (2 Kings 19:21) The Daughter of Jerusalem also "shakes her head behind you."

Yes. The LORD asks, "Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!" (2 Kings 19:22) The LORD answers His own question.
Tirhakah, king of Cush, is the one Sennacherib was warned about (2 Kings 19:9). But the LORD says the taunting and pride were aimed "Against the Holy One of Israel!" (2 Kings 19:22)
The king of Babylon isn't named anywhere in these verses. The LORD asks who Sennacherib has taunted, and the answer is, "Against the Holy One of Israel!" (2 Kings 19:22)
The LORD says the opposite. He asks, "Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it." (2 Kings 19:25) So Sennacherib's conquests were not apart from His plan.

That's right. The LORD says, "Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it. Now I have brought it to pass, that you should crush fortified cities into piles of rubble." (2 Kings 19:25) Sennacherib thought he did it all on his own, and the LORD has been planning it for a long time.

explanations.answer: Put a hook in his nose and send him back
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, "I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came." (2 Kings 19:28) Sennacherib came in loud, and he gets led out.

explanations.answer: Let him take the city for a season
explanations.explanation: That's not in the LORD's word. He says He will put His hook in Sennacherib's nose and "send you back the way you came." (2 Kings 19:28) Jerusalem isn't handed over for a season or for any other length of time.

explanations.answer: Hand his kingdom to the king of Cush
explanations.explanation: The LORD says nothing about giving his kingdom to anyone. He says, "I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came." (2 Kings 19:28) Tirhakah, king of Cush, doesn't get a prize here.

That's the sign. The LORD says, "But in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit." (2 Kings 19:29) Two years of food that grows on its own, then a full planting season.

explanations.answer: Assyria will come back for them
explanations.explanation: Not in the sign. The LORD says, "But in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit." (2 Kings 19:29) Planting vineyards is what people do when they're staying put.

explanations.answer: They'll have to leave the land
explanations.explanation: The sign points the other direction. The LORD says that in the third year, "you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit." (2 Kings 19:29) Nobody plants vineyards on their way out the door.
The LORD says no arrows at all. He says Sennacherib "will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it." (2 Kings 19:32) Not one, friend.
That's right. The LORD says the king of Assyria "will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it." (2 Kings 19:32) That's not one arrow, a shield, or a siege ramp (2 Kings 19:32).

David is right. The LORD says, "I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David." (2 Kings 19:34) David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is the servant He names.
Moses led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12:51), but he's not the name in this verse. The LORD says He'll save the city "for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David." (2 Kings 19:34)

Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), but the LORD doesn't name him here. He says He'll defend the city "for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David." (2 Kings 19:34) Same kind of word, "servant," different man.
Yes. "So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there." (2 Kings 19:36) The LORD said he'd go back the way he came, and he does (2 Kings 19:33).
The text doesn't send him to Egypt. It says he "broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there." (2 Kings 19:36) He heads home, not farther down the road.
Damascus isn't named in this passage. The text says Sennacherib "returned to Nineveh and stayed there." (2 Kings 19:36) Home was the destination.
Esar-haddon is the one. After Adrammelech and Sharezer put their father to the sword, the text says, "And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place." (2 Kings 19:37) The throne passes to a third son.
Adrammelech is one of the sons who put Sennacherib to the sword. The text says he and Sharezer "escaped to the land of Ararat." (2 Kings 19:37) The one who reigns is "his son Esar-haddon."

Sharezer is the other son in that attack, along with Adrammelech, and they escaped to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19:37). He doesn't take the throne. The text says, "And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place." (2 Kings 19:37)
